record.paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
record.context_brief: Competing decay paths for high-K isomers
record.original_question: For tunneling decay from high-K to low-K isomers, which decay path dominates: the path through large-amplitude collective motion in the triaxial shape degree of freedom or the path through motion in the orientation degree of freedom of the angular-momentum vector relative to the principal axes of the body-fixed frame?

evidence.quote: The tunneling decay from high-K to low-K isomers is also interesting [65], because it poses a unique question as to which of the two competing decay paths dominates; one through LACM in the triaxial shape degree of freedom and the other in the orientation degree of freedom of the angular momentum vector (with respect to the principal axes of the body-fixed frame).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an axially deformed atomic nucleus carrying a high value of K, the projection of the total angular momentum on the body-fixed symmetry axis. Such a "high-K isomer" can decay to a state of low K (a "low-K isomer") only by mechanisms that effectively change K, since K is approximately conserved for axially symmetric shapes. Within a microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion (LACM), at least two qualitatively different tunneling decay paths compete:

(i) a path in which the nucleus tunnels through a barrier in the triaxial shape degree of freedom (parameterized, e.g., by the triaxiality parameter γ), evolving its intrinsic shape from axial to triaxial and back while changing K;

(ii) a path in which the shape remains essentially fixed but the orientation of the angular-momentum vector relative to the three principal axes of the body-fixed frame undergoes large-amplitude motion (a "wobbling/tilting" path that reorients J with respect to the symmetry axis).

Determine, on the basis of a microscopic LACM treatment that includes both the triaxial shape collective coordinate and the angular-momentum orientation collective coordinate on equal footing, which of the two paths above dominates the tunneling decay rate from high-K to low-K isomers, and characterize the regimes (mass region, K, excitation energy, softness of γ) in which one path dominates over the other.
artifact.status_search_result: The literature identifies both mechanisms — γ-tunneling through triaxial shapes and reorientation of the angular-momentum vector (Coriolis/tilted-axis mixing) — as competing K-mixing channels for high-K isomer decay, with no consensus on which dominates in general. Recent works (e.g., superfluid tunneling models and studies in the A~180 region) treat each mechanism separately rather than within a unified microscopic LACM that determines the dominant path, suggesting the question remains open.

status_evidence.title: Decay of high-K isomers in a superfluid tunneling model
status_evidence.snippet: Decay rates are discussed in terms of a tunneling model where high-K (isomeric) and low-K states interact via fluctuations towards triaxial nuclear shapes.
status_evidence.claim: γ-tunneling through triaxial shapes is treated as one mechanism for K-mixing, but its dominance over orientation-based mixing is not established.

status_evidence.title: Metastable States in Atomic Nuclei: High-K Isomers
status_evidence.snippet: Two mechanisms are suggested: Coriolis mixing of different K values, and tunneling through a potential barrier in the γ degree of freedom.
status_evidence.claim: Two competing K-mixing mechanisms (orientation-based Coriolis mixing and triaxial γ-tunneling) coexist in the literature without a settled answer as to which dominates.

status_evidence.title: Effect of a Triaxial Nuclear Shape on Proton Tunneling
status_evidence.snippet: Triaxial shape degree of freedom plays a role in tunneling decays.
status_evidence.claim: Demonstrates relevance of triaxial shape but does not resolve dominance vs. orientation degree of freedom.
